architecture: A chi v5 HTTP service for a logistics carrier: database/sql over Postgres, the authenticated actor carried on the request context by a session middleware, encoding/json bodies, and os/exec for PDF label work.

cases.architecture: chi v5 router; GET /v1/shipments assembles its WHERE clause from whichever console filters arrived, then runs it with database/sql.
cases.why: Every other filter appends its value to args and emits a $n placeholder, but the free-text `q` parameter is formatted directly into the predicate text with fmt.Sprintf and then concatenated into the statement that QueryContext executes. A single quote in `q` closes the ILIKE literal, so the caller controls the rest of the WHERE clause and can UNION in any table the API role can read, across every tenant. The tenant_id binding on lines 52-53 is correct and does nothing to help, because the injected text is appended after it.

cases.architecture: chi v5 router; GET /v1/shipments/lookup assembles its WHERE clause from whichever scan-gun filters arrived, then runs it with database/sql.
cases.why: The statement is still built by fmt.Sprintf and strings.Join over a dynamic clause list, which is exactly the shape of its vulnerable sibling, but every Sprintf here formats only a placeholder index: the scanned term travels as the value "%"+q+"%" in args and the predicate text only ever says $n. The ORDER BY column comes from lookupSortColumns, so the caller's sort key indexes a map of fixed column literals and is then discarded, and LIMIT/OFFSET are bound rather than interpolated. No caller-controlled byte reaches the statement text.

cases.architecture: chi v5 router; GET /v1/shipments/{shipmentID} loads one row for the console detail drawer, behind a session middleware that puts the actor on the context.
cases.why: The handler proves the caller is authenticated and then never uses that fact: the row is selected on `WHERE s.id = $1` alone, with the actor's TenantID not in the predicate. Shipment ids are opaque but they are handed out in search results, webhooks and label keys, so any signed-in operator on any tenant can read another tenant's consignee name, address and declared value by substituting the id. The query even scans tenant_id into the response body, which makes the missing comparison plain.

cases.architecture: chi v5 router; GET /v1/shipments/{shipmentID}/events loads the tracking history for the console detail drawer, behind a session middleware that puts the actor on the context.
cases.why: The event query really is scoped by id alone — `WHERE e.shipment_id = $1` with no tenant column, because tracking_events has none — which looks identical to the defect in its sibling. It is correct because assertShipmentVisible has already resolved the same id against `shipments WHERE id = $1 AND tenant_id = $2` using the actor from the context, and returns ErrNotFound for a shipment on another tenant, so the handler cannot reach the second query with an id it is not entitled to.

cases.architecture: chi v5 router; GET /v1/labels/documents streams a rendered carrier PDF off the shared spool volume using the storage key the batch API returned.
cases.why: The `key` query parameter is joined onto the spool root and opened with no confinement check. filepath.Join normalises ".." rather than rejecting it, so key=../../../../etc/passwd resolves outside the spool and the file is streamed back with Content-Disposition attachment. The comment's assumption — that the key was minted by the renderer — is not enforced anywhere, and the key arrives from the client on every request. Any authenticated operator gets arbitrary read of whatever the service account can open, including every other tenant's labels.

cases.architecture: chi v5 router; GET /v1/labels/archives streams a nightly depot archive off the shared spool volume using the archive key the packer returned.
cases.why: The caller-supplied key is still passed straight into filepath.Join with the spool root, which is the same construct that makes its sibling exploitable. It is safe because resolveInsideSpool never returns the joined path directly: it resolves both the root and the candidate through EvalSymlinks and then requires filepath.Rel(root, candidate) not to be ".." or to start with "../", so anything that climbs out of the spool — including a symlink planted inside it — is reported as a 404 before os.Open is reached.

cases.architecture: chi v5 router; POST /v1/carriers/{carrierCode}/callback-test fires a sample webhook at the operator's configured endpoint and shows them the reply, behind session + admin middleware.
cases.why: callback_url comes out of the request body and is used verbatim as the destination of a server-side POST, with the status code and the first 8 KB of the reply handed back to the caller. Nothing constrains the scheme, the host or the port, so a tenant admin can reach 169.254.169.254, the Postgres host, or any service on the cluster network and read the response — this is a fully readable SSRF, not a blind one. Being admin-only is not a mitigation in a multi-tenant product where every customer has an admin.

cases.architecture: chi v5 router; POST /v1/carriers/{carrierCode}/rate-probe calls the carrier's regional rate endpoint the operator nominated and shows them the reply, behind session + admin middleware.
cases.why: This handler also takes a full URL from the request body, performs a server-side request to it, and echoes the body back — the same shape as its sibling. It is correct because the parsed URL must be https, must carry no userinfo, must use port 443 or none, and its Hostname() must be an exact key in the per-carrier rateEndpointHosts set — exact equality, so a suffix like dhl.com.example.net does not pass — and the client's CheckRedirect refuses to follow a 302, which closes the usual escape where an allowed host bounces the probe somewhere internal.

cases.architecture: chi v5 router; POST /v1/manifests/{batchRef}/sheet merges the per-parcel label PDFs on the spool volume into one driver manifest by shelling out to pdfunite.
cases.why: batchRef is a chi path parameter, so it is caller-controlled text, and it is interpolated with fmt.Sprintf into a string that is then handed to /bin/sh -c. A path segment can carry semicolons, backticks, $( ) and percent-encoded spaces, all of which the shell honours, so a request to /v1/manifests/A%3Bcurl%20.../sheet runs arbitrary commands as the API service account. The glob is a real reason to want a shell, but it is not a reason to build the command line by concatenation.

cases.architecture: chi v5 router; POST /v1/manifests/{batchRef}/export merges the per-parcel label PDFs on the spool volume into the customs copy by invoking pdfunite.
cases.why: A caller-controlled path parameter still reaches exec.CommandContext, and the file even builds a joined command string for the failure log, which is what makes it tempting. It is correct because batchRef must match ^[A-Z0-9]{4,24}$ before anything happens, the glob is expanded in-process by filepath.Glob so no shell is involved, and the binary is invoked in argv form at an absolute path with one element per file — there is no interpreter to inject into, and the regex also rules out a leading dash, so the value cannot be read as a flag.

cases.architecture: chi v5 router; a middleware authenticates the public carrier status callbacks at POST /v1/carriers/webhooks/{carrier} by HMAC over the raw body with a per-carrier shared secret.
cases.why: The computed HMAC is compared against the attacker-supplied header with Go's string !=, which returns as soon as two bytes differ and so leaks how many leading hex characters were correct. These routes are public and the signature is the only authentication on them, so the comparison is the whole security boundary; a reviewer would require crypto/hmac.Equal or crypto/subtle here. The comment reasons about length and case, which is not what makes a comparison safe.

cases.architecture: chi v5 router; a middleware authenticates the public 3PL inventory callbacks at POST /v1/partners/webhooks/{partner} by HMAC over timestamp and raw body with a per-partner issued key.
cases.why: There is a plain != comparison of a credential-shaped header value on line 51, which is what makes this tempting, but the value compared is the key *id* — a public identifier printed on the partner's settings page and already revealed by the map lookup on the line above — not the secret. The secret comparison is hmac.Equal over raw bytes, the signed material includes the timestamp so an old signature cannot be replayed onto a fresh body, and a malformed hex signature is rejected before any comparison.
